title: Week 6: Feature Engineering
text:
Key Concepts

A linear model is linear in the features supplied to it. Transforming those features allows nonlinear relationships, group differences, and spatial heterogeneity.
A coefficient’s interpretation depends on whether the outcome or predictor is logged, squared, or interacted with a category.
Evaluate a model of log(rent) by back-transforming predictions to dollars before calculating RMSE against rent.
Categorical variables use a reference group; changing that group changes coefficient comparisons, not fitted predictions.
Fixed effects capture shared group-level differences, but they do not identify their causes and cannot directly predict a category absent from training.
For prediction, compare candidate models with out-of-sample CV RMSE. A low p-value or strong training fit is not enough, and an association is not necessarily causal.

title: Week 6: Feature Engineering
text:
Note

1. What Is Feature Engineering?
A linear regression can draw only a straight-line relationship through the features it receives. Feature engineering means deciding what information and transformations to supply. A model can remain linear in its coefficients while using log(income), I(bldg_age^2), distance bands, interactions, or district indicators to represent relationships that are not simply straight lines in the original variables.
For prediction, the practical question is whether the new features lower error on unseen observations. For interpretation, the practical question is what a one-unit change in each transformed feature means. Neither a predictive improvement nor a regression coefficient by itself establishes causation.


2. Data, Baseline Model, and Fixed CV Folds
The class example uses approximately 377 Philadelphia census tracts from the 2023 ACS five-year data. The tract geometries are projected to EPSG:2272, whose units are feet. The variables are:



Variable
Meaning




rent
Median gross rent, in dollars


income
Median household income


pct_renter
Percentage of renter-occupied households


bldg_age
Building age, calculated as 2023 - yr_builtE


dist_ch_mi
Distance from the tract to City Hall, in miles



The baseline specification and result log are:
f0 <- rent ~ income + pct_renter + bldg_age + dist_ch_mi
m0 <- lm(f0, data = tracts)
model_log <- tibble(
  model = "m0",
  added = "baseline",
  cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f0, tracts)
)
model_log
f0 is a formula, not a fitted model; lm() fits it. summary(m0) reports estimated coefficients. Here, model_log is a table of model results—“log” does not mean logarithm. Baseline 10-fold CV RMSE was approximately $265; lower is better.
The comparison uses one reproducible set of ten folds. In each round, nine folds train the model and the remaining fold supplies unseen validation observations:
set.seed(5080)
folds <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = nrow(tracts)))

cv_rmse <- function(f, data, log_outcome = FALSE) {
  preds <- numeric(nrow(data))
  for (k in 1:10) {
    m <- lm(f, data = data[folds != k, ])
    p <- predict(m, newdata = data[folds == k, ])
    if (log_outcome) p <- exp(p) # Return predictions to dollars.
    preds[folds == k] <- p
  }
  sqrt(mean((data$rent - preds)^2))
}
Every candidate model must use the same folds for a fair comparison. This helper assumes data has the same row count and order as the data used to create folds; rebuild the folds if those rows change. The examples in this note depend on the class tracts object and are not run when this note is rendered.


3. Log Transformations

Why log a predictor?
Income is often right-skewed. log(income) compresses high values and makes equal proportional changes approximately equally spaced. A $20,000 change from $20,000 to $40,000 is economically different from a $20,000 change from $180,000 to $200,000, even though their absolute differences match.
ggplot(tracts, aes(income)) + geom_histogram(bins = 40)
ggplot(tracts, aes(log(income))) + geom_histogram(bins = 40)


Four common model forms








Model form
Formula example
Coefficient interpretation




Level–level
y ~ x
A one-unit increase in X corresponds to a \(\beta\)-unit change in Y.


Level–log
y ~ log(x)
A 1% increase in X corresponds to approximately a \(\beta/100\)-unit change in Y.


Log–level
log(y) ~ x
A one-unit increase in X corresponds to approximately a \(100\beta\)% change in Y.


Log–log
log(y) ~ log(x)
A 1% increase in X corresponds to approximately a \(\beta\)% change in Y; \(\beta\) is an elasticity.



For rent ~ log(income) + ..., suppose the estimated income coefficient is 502.1787. A 1% income increase is associated with about $5.02 higher predicted monthly rent. For a 10% increase, use the exact log change:
\[
502.1787\log(1.10)\approx\$47.86.
\]
For log(rent) ~ log(income) + ..., a coefficient of 0.36334 means that a 1% income increase is associated with approximately a 0.363% rent increase. In a log–level model, the exact percentage change for a one-unit increase in X is \(100(e^\beta-1)\)%, rather than exactly \(100\beta\)%.


Zeros and negative values
log(0) is -Inf. For nonnegative counts such as crimes, trees, or 311 calls, log1p(x) computes \(\log(1+x)\) and retains zero observations:
log(0)
log1p(c(0, 1, 10, 100))
For small counts, the ordinary percentage-change interpretation of log(x) does not transfer exactly to log1p(x). Negative values require a transformation chosen for the substantive data context.


A logged outcome must be evaluated in dollars
A training residual RMSE of about 0.1885 for log(rent) is on a log scale. It cannot be compared directly with a training residual RMSE of about $259.55 for an unlogged rent model. To compare predictive accuracy, return each logged prediction to dollars, then compute CV RMSE against observed rent:
f_logy <- log(rent) ~ log(income) + pct_renter +
  bldg_age + dist_ch_mi
cv_rmse(f_logy, tracts, log_outcome = TRUE)
Because \(\exp(E[\log Y])\neq E[Y]\), simply exponentiating a fitted log outcome does not automatically give an unbiased prediction of mean rent; the note’s back-transformation is for comparison on the original dollar scale.



4. Squared Terms and Curvature
If a flexible smooth on a scatterplot bends while a straight geom_smooth(method = "lm") line misses that pattern, a quadratic term may help:
f_sq <- rent ~ log(income) + pct_renter + bldg_age +
  I(bldg_age^2) + dist_ch_mi
m_sq <- lm(f_sq, data = tracts)
In an R formula, I(bldg_age^2) means the literal square; ^ otherwise has special formula syntax. For \(Y=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2x^2\), the marginal slope at a particular \(x\) is \(\beta_1+2\beta_2x\). Do not interpret \(\beta_1\) or \(\beta_2\) in isolation as a constant effect. A positive linear term with a negative square makes an inverted U; a negative linear term with a positive square makes a U.
The turning point is \(x^*=-\beta_1/(2\beta_2)\). In the class example, the building-age coefficients were about \(-28.00445\) and \(+0.1823244\), giving a minimum around 76.8 years. That is near the upper end of the observed age range of roughly 5–85 years. The pre-1940 Census category is encoded as “1939 or earlier,” which bunches old buildings together; this fitted curve is not a natural law. Predictions far outside the observed age range can be implausible.


5. Categorical Variables and Reference Groups
Use categorical features for naturally distinct groups, such as zoning, planning district, or housing type. A numeric variable can also be grouped if the relationship seems to change in steps rather than smoothly. For example:
tracts <- tracts %>% mutate(
  renter_band = cut(
    pct_renter,
    breaks = c(0, 33, 66, 100),
    labels = c("Mostly owners", "Mixed", "Mostly renters"),
    include.lowest = TRUE
  )
)
tracts %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(renter_band)
The three example bands contain 88, 210, and 79 tracts. cut() uses numeric break points, case_when() supports custom rules, and factor() tells R to treat values as categories. With an intercept and \(k\) categories, the model normally uses \(k-1\) dummy variables, generated by model.matrix().
If Core is the reference in a distance-ring model, coefficients ringInner = -122.2774 and ringOuter = -164.1935 mean that, holding other features fixed, predicted rent is about $122.28 lower in Inner and $164.19 lower in Outer than in Core. They do not mean that rent in Outer is negative. Changing the reference group changes coefficient comparisons, not the fitted predictions:
tracts_r <- tracts %>% mutate(ring = relevel(ring, ref = "Outer"))
Binning sacrifices information: replacing continuous dist_ch_mi with Core/Inner/Outer treats distinct distances within the same band alike. If the true relationship is smooth, this can worsen prediction.


6. Interactions: Different Slopes by Group
An interaction is useful when the relationship between X and Y differs by group:
f_int <- rent ~ log(income) * ring + pct_renter +
  bldg_age + I(bldg_age^2)
m_int <- lm(f_int, data = tracts)
In R formula syntax, a * b expands to a + b + a:b, whereas a:b adds only the interaction. With Core as the reference, the log(income) slope is 653.6974. The Inner interaction changes it by −219.1028, giving about 434.59; the Outer interaction changes it by −244.4214, giving about 409.28. Because the outcome is rent in dollars and income is logged, a 1% income increase corresponds to approximately the group-specific slope divided by 100 dollars of monthly rent.
Interacting every feature with every group increases the number of parameters quickly. With only about 377 tracts, that can overfit.


7. Place Fixed Effects

7.1 District intercepts
A place fixed effect gives each district its own intercept through a categorical district variable. It can absorb shared, unmeasured background differences—such as reputation, schools, transit, and history—but cannot reveal which of those mechanisms matters. The class example assigns each tract to the Philadelphia planning district with which it has the greatest area overlap, across 18 planning districts:
tracts <- tracts %>%
  st_join(
    districts %>% select(district = dist_name),
    largest = TRUE
  ) %>%
  mutate(district = factor(district))

f_fe <- rent ~ log(income) + pct_renter + bldg_age +
  I(bldg_age^2) + district
m_fe <- lm(f_fe, data = tracts)
In this example, the log(income) coefficient fell from about 519.74 before district effects to 427.39 after them. The earlier estimate mixed between-district and within-district differences; with district intercepts, the coefficient primarily compares tracts within districts. This change does not automatically establish a causal effect.


7.2 The unseen-category problem in CV
A fixed-effect model cannot directly predict a district level that did not appear in its training fold. count(district) revealed that Lower South had only one tract; a 10-fold CV round could place that one tract entirely in validation, causing predict() to fail. The class solution merged districts with fewer than ten tracts into a nearby district for a CV-ready variable:
small <- tracts %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(district) %>% filter(n < 10 | is.na(district)) %>%
  pull(district)

is_small <- tracts$district %in% small | is.na(tracts$district)
nearest <- st_nearest_feature(tracts[is_small, ], tracts[!is_small, ])

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(district_cv = as.character(district))
tracts$district_cv[is_small] <-
  as.character(tracts$district[!is_small][nearest])
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(district_cv = factor(district_cv))
At least about 10 observations per group is a useful 10-fold CV rule of thumb; more is safer. Other approaches include combining rare levels into “Other” (for example, with fct_lump_min()), although that may not make geographic sense, or using coarser spatial units. District IDs such as 1–18 are labels, not a continuous numeric predictor, so they must be represented as a factor.


7.3 Fixed effects versus measured spatial features

District fixed effects answer which districts differ in baseline rent, capturing leftover shared district variation. They do not explain the mechanism or generalize directly to a new district.
Spatial features such as distance to transit or parks and nearby crime describe measurable attributes. They can reveal associations with those attributes and may generalize conditionally to new locations.

Both can be used together: measured spatial features may explain some differences, while district effects absorb remaining shared district variation. The class note points ahead to nearby-neighbor (kNN) features on October 16.



8. Model Comparison: 10-Fold CV RMSE

title: Assignment3: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
I analyze Alfred Lubrano’s 2018 WHYY / Philadelphia Inquirer article, “New Census figures on Philly neighborhoods show inequality, high numbers of whites living in poverty.” The article reports that Eastwick’s poverty rate increased from 12 percent in the 2006–2010 ACS period to 26 percent in the 2013–2017 ACS period. It also states that the newer figures come from the American Community Survey (ACS) five-year estimates.
The article reports results for Philadelphia neighborhoods, but neighborhoods such as Eastwick are not official Census geographies. The Census Bureau publishes ACS data for Census tracts, which have GEOIDs and defined boundaries. Since the article does not provide its tract-to-neighborhood crosswalk or boundary file, I cannot exactly reproduce its neighborhood-level estimates. Therefore, I reconstruct and test the article’s general poverty-change claim at the Census-tract level for Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania.
Source article: https://whyy.org/articles/new-census-figures-on-philly-neighborhoods-show-inequality-high-numbers-of-whites-living-in-poverty/



I use ACS detailed table B17001, Poverty Status in the Past 12 Months by Sex by Age. The table provides a poverty count and its margin of error, as well as the population for whom poverty status is determined.

B17001_001: Total population for whom poverty status is determined. I use this as the denominator.
B17001_002: Population with income in the past 12 months below the poverty level. I use this as the numerator.

For each Census tract, the poverty rate will be calculated as:
\[
\text{Poverty rate} =
\frac{\text{B17001\_002}}{\text{B17001\_001}}
\]
These variables match the article’s general discussion of overall poverty rates. They do not measure poverty only for a specific age group, sex, or race. The article also discusses white poverty in Holmesburg, but that would require a separate race-specific analysis and a clear definition of “white” that the article does not provide. I therefore focus this analysis on overall poverty.


Show code
# Get data
get_poverty <- function(yr) {
  get_acs(
    geography = "tract",
    variables = c(
      below_poverty = "B17001_002",
      total = "B17001_001"
    ),
    state = "PA",
    county = "Philadelphia",
    year = yr,
    survey = "acs5",
    output = "wide"
  ) %>%
    mutate(period = paste0(yr - 4, "-", yr)
  )
}

# Retrieve and combine tract-level poverty data.
poverty_change <- bind_rows(
  get_poverty(2010),
  get_poverty(2017)
)




Show code
poverty_change %>%
  count(period, name = "Number of Census tracts") %>%
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("ACS period", "Number of Census tracts")
  )



Table 1. Census tracts retrieved from ACS 5-year data


ACS period
Number of Census tracts




2006-2010
384


2013-2017
384








I use the 2010 and 2017 ACS five-year releases because they match the two periods discussed in the article: 2006–2010 and 2013–2017. I use acs5 because tract-level data are available in the five-year ACS, while the one-year ACS does not provide tract estimates.
The article does not explain exactly which Census table, poverty-rate denominator, or neighborhood boundaries it used. I therefore use table B17001 and calculate poverty rates for Census tracts in Philadelphia County. This cannot exactly reproduce the article’s neighborhood results because neighborhoods do not have official Census boundaries. I also match tracts by GEOID before comparing the two periods.
The two ACS periods do not overlap, so they do not use the same survey years. However, each estimate still represents a five-year average. For this reason, the results show changes in estimated tract poverty rates, not changes experienced by the same individual residents.

The ACS reports 90 percent margins of error. I divide each MOE by 1.645 to calculate its standard error, combine the two standard errors to calculate the standard error of the difference, and multiply by 1.645 to obtain the 90 percent margin of error for the change.


Show code

  filter(
    !is.na(`poverty_rate_2006-2010`),
    !is.na(`poverty_rate_2013-2017`),

    se_2 = `poverty_rate_moe_2013-2017` / 1.645,

    moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,

    z = change / se_diff,
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645,

    change_direction = case_when(

      significant & change < 0 ~ "Significant decrease",
      TRUE ~ "Not distinguishable from zero"

text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
In this analysis, I look at median gross rent across counties in New York State. I compare the margins of error for these estimates to identify which counties’ rent data are measured most and least reliably.

The only low-confidence county, Hamilton County, has a population of 5,102. This pattern suggests that median gross rent estimates are less reliable in counties with smaller populations, although the low-confidence category contains only one county.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
This analysis shows that New York’s smallest counties tend to have the least reliable median gross rent estimates. Hamilton County is the clearest example: its estimated median gross rent is $860 with a margin of error of $95, or about 11.0 percent. It is the only low-confidence county under the 10 percent cutoff and has only 5,102 residents. Schuyler County has the next-highest relative margin of error at 8.7 percent, followed by Greene County at 8.0 percent.
These differences reflect how the American Community Survey works. The ACS draws estimates from a sample rather than counting every household. Smaller counties generally contain fewer sampled households, so a small number of responses can have a larger effect on their estimates. In these results, high-confidence counties average about 381,479 residents, compared with 41,178 in moderate-confidence counties and 5,102 in the low-confidence county. This pattern indicates that estimates become less precise as county population decreases.
If a state agency allocated housing assistance using median gross rent while treating every estimate as equally certain, small rural counties could be harmed. An underestimated rent could make a county appear less burdened and cause it to receive too little funding, while an overestimate could divert funds from places with greater need. Renters in Hamilton, Schuyler, and Greene Counties may therefore be especially vulnerable. Agencies should consider both the estimates and their margins of error, and they should avoid making major funding decisions based on small differences that may reflect sampling uncertainty.

  mutate(fitted_m2 = fitted(m2),
         resid_m2  = residuals(m2))

ggplot(tracts, aes(x = rent_cv, y = abs(resid_m2))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "CV of the median rent estimate (%)",
       y = "Size of the model's miss ($)",
       title = "Are the biggest misses in the noisiest tracts?") +
  theme_minimal()








Stop and look: If a tract’s rent estimate has a CV of 35%, how much of the model’s miss there could be survey noise rather than a model failure? What does that mean for flagging “tracts with rents above expectation”?

text:
Part 6: Fit vs. prediction






WarningTwo different CVs



Week 3 CV = coefficient of variation: how noisy is one estimate? Today’s CV = cross-validation: how well does a model predict data it hasn’t seen? Same letters, unrelated ideas.



6A: One train/test split

set.seed(5080)
n <- nrow(tracts)
train_idx <- sample(1:n, size = 0.8 * n)

train_data <- tracts[train_idx, ]
test_data  <- tracts[-train_idx, ]

m2_train <- lm(med_rentE ~ med_incE + pct_renter + pct_ba + n_stations,
               data = train_data)

test_pred <- predict(m2_train, newdata = test_data)

rmse_train <- sqrt(mean(residuals(m2_train)^2))
rmse_test  <- sqrt(mean((test_data$med_rentE - test_pred)^2))

c(train = rmse_train, test = rmse_test)

   train     test 
260.6789 278.8252 


Stop and look: Which RMSE is larger? Why would you expect that? In words: “The model’s typical miss on tracts it hasn’t seen is about $___ per month.”
Change the seed to any other number and rerun the chunk. Did the test RMSE change? That’s why one split isn’t enough.


6B: 10-fold cross-validation
caret wants a plain data frame, so drop the geometry first. (The geometry isn’t a predictor, and train() will choke on it.)

model_df <- tracts %>% st_drop_geometry()

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

set.seed(5080)
cv_m1 <- train(med_rentE ~ med_incE,
               data = model_df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)

set.seed(5080)
cv_m2 <- train(med_rentE ~ med_incE + pct_renter + pct_ba + n_stations,
               data = model_df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)

7B: The map
The residuals are already a column in an sf data frame. Mapping them is one geom_sf() away.

ggplot(tracts) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = resid_m2), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "grey95", high = "#b2182b",
                       midpoint = 0, labels = scales::dollar) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Where the rent model is wrong",
       subtitle = "Red = rent higher than predicted · Blue = lower than predicted",
       fill = "Residual")








Stop and look: If the errors were random, the map would look speckled. Does it? Where do the reds sit together? What might those places have in common that the model doesn’t know about?
Write down your answer. We’ll come back to it in Weeks 6 and 7.

title: Week 5 In-Class Lab: Where the Model Is Wrong
text:
Part 8: The Challenge
Your team’s job: build the best model for predicting tract median rent, then use it to answer the agency’s question.

Rules

The grade is 10-fold CV RMSE. Use model_df (or tracts) and run set.seed(5080) directly before train(), exactly as in Part 6B, so every team is tested on the same folds.
Don’t drop rows. If you add a variable with missing values, you change the folds and the comparison stops being fair. Fill the gaps or choose a different variable.
You may add any ACS variables (use load_variables(2023, "acs5") to browse) and any spatial feature you can build with Week 4 tools: distances, buffers, counts.
You may not use anything built from rent itself. That rules out med_rentM, rent_cv, rent burden (B25071), and the rent distribution tables (B25063). Ask yourself: would the agency have this variable for a tract whose rent it’s trying to predict? If not, using it is cheating the test. That’s called leakage.



Deliver

Your CV RMSE, in dollars, written as a sentence.
One feature you added, and why. What did you think it would capture that the census variables miss? Did it help?
One coefficient, read twice. Pick a variable in your final model and give its β̂ reading and its ŷ reading in one sentence each.
The agency’s list. Using your final model fit to all tracts, find the five tracts with the largest positive residuals (rent well above expectation). For each, report the residual and the rent CV. Which of the five would you tell the agency to trust, and which might be fog?
Your residual map. Did your added features make the clusters from Part 7B shrink?

Replace med_incE with log(med_incE). Does the curve in Part 2 straighten? Does CV RMSE improve? How do you read the new coefficient?
